observations.statement: The paper states two complementary quasi-experimental strategies for the same geography: variation in where bridges are built (upstream versus downstream of tributary confluences) for long-run local effects, and variation in when bridges open for dynamic effects over decades at the county scale.

For the confluence design the identifying assumption is written as a formal conditional mean-zero condition on the error given nearest-tributary fixed effects, the downstream indicator, river-distance and their interaction.

Threats to the confluence design are listed explicitly: faster water downstream favouring industry, ports forming downstream, Y-shaped confluences giving upstream areas more water access, and flooding upstream. Each is named before the placebo evidence is presented.

For the timing design the identifying assumption is stated formally as exogeneity of the timing of changes in bridge distance to short-run deviations from county-specific quadratic trends, with the window of leads and lags over which it is assumed to hold spelled out.

The direction of bias from possible policy timing is discussed in both directions: bridges built as stimulus after slow growth or at the start of a boom would bias upward, while bridges built after decades of growth would bias downward via regression to the mean.

The author explains why only reduced-form effects of confluence position are reported: position predicts both road and rail distance and historical and contemporary access, so separating channels would need restrictive assumptions; the coefficient is interpreted as a net effect of distance since the historical era.

Exogeneity of bridge opening timing is argued with historical narrative: named examples of decades-long lags between charter or proposal and completion, plus the observation that a bridge's network effect is realized on opening day.

Bridge data are hand-assembled from the National Bridge Inventory, cross-checked with satellite imagery and contemporary and historical sources; census outcomes come from NHGIS, ICPSR county files and IPUMS full-count microdata; river alignments from ESRI and USGS datasets.

The unit of analysis is stated as the census tract (cross-section in a single census year) for the location design and the county (decadal balanced panel over a century and a half, in fixed baseline boundaries) for the timing design.

The river sample is truncated at named upstream limits, justified by river meandering and an engineer's assessment of where major works become necessary; results are said to be insensitive to an alternative truncation point.

Tracts far from confluences are excluded using a threshold chosen by RD optimal bandwidth selection run on three key demeaned outcomes, fixing the threshold as the minimum of the three selected bandwidths for consistency; confluences matched to only one tract are dropped.

County boundary changes are handled by remapping all data to baseline-year boundaries: separated counties are re-aggregated by summing totals or area-weighted means, merged counties are split proportionally by area; microdata households are assigned with area weights.
Each regression table reports the number of observations, and the tract tables additionally report the number of tributary clusters in every column.
The choice of panel start year is justified as a compromise between spatial and temporal coverage, with a footnote reporting that results hold for alternative start and end years.

Major tributary confluences are defined by a flow-increment rule from hydrological model data, and river position is measured in signed river-kilometres by assigning tracts the nearest river reach, isolating the component parallel to flow.
The panel treatment is the change in log distance from county centroid to the nearest bridge, entered as contemporaneous and lagged changes; lead changes are added in diagnostic columns only.

Average agricultural land value is used as the proxy for total economic activity; a footnote derives the link between land value and output elasticities under simple assumptions and explains why average rather than total land value is preferred over a very long panel.

Distance to a bridge is explicitly framed as a proxy for distance to a land transport route, validated in modern data against distance to rail and road and against historical market access measures from another study.
observations.locator: Section 3 Bridges and land transport infrastructure; Figure 4; footnote 18

observations.statement: Table notes for the tract regressions describe the fixed effects and controls, the sample inclusion rules and exclusions, the triangular kernel weights, and the cluster bootstrap by nearest confluence with the number of replications.

The county panel table notes list year and county fixed effects and county-specific quadratic trends, state that the sample is unweighted with constant baseline boundaries, and report clustering by county with spatial robustness within a stated radius; joint p-values for lead and lag groups are rows in the table.

The placebo table is organised with a bottom panel of row labels (outcome year, sample, historical controls) so columns move from the main sample to the matched historical subsample, then placebo outcome, then main outcome with historical controls.
Regression tables report neither R-squared nor the dependent variable mean; sample means of key outcomes appear only in the summary statistics table.

Because outcomes and bridge distance are spatially correlated, tract-level inference uses a bootstrap resampling whole tributary confluences, described as treating each confluence as one observation; the small number of confluences is acknowledged and addressed with permutation tests.

Panel standard errors are clustered by county to allow arbitrary serial correlation, cited to Bertrand et al. and Angrist and Pischke and called conservative for a long horizon, and are additionally made robust to spatial correlation within a fixed radius using Conley standard errors with code adapted from Hsiang.

Two shock-based inference exercises are reported: random flipping of confluence orientation for half the confluences under the null, and Borusyak-Hull style simulation of counterfactual bridge opening dates with recomputed distance histories; realized estimates are compared with simulated distributions in appendix figures.
observations.locator: Section 4.3; Section 5.3 Non-random exposure; Appendix Figures C17, C25; footnote 28

observations.statement: Descriptive nonparametric fits use Bayesian-bootstrapped confidence intervals with Dirichlet weights clustered by state (national data) or by confluence (river sample), with the number of iterations and references given in footnotes and figure notes.

Pre-bridge-era county outcomes matched to modern tracts serve as placebo outcomes in a main-text table; the same table re-estimates main effects on the matchable subsample and with historical outcomes as controls, and the measurement error from county-to-tract assignment is acknowledged.

The author explains that a McCrary-style density test at confluences would fail by construction because tract density tracks population density, which is itself an outcome, so no density test is reported.

Lead coefficients on future changes in bridge distance are shown in separate table columns with a joint p-value row, plotted with a reversed y-axis in an event-style figure, and the lag length is chosen per outcome so that lead coefficients are closest to zero.

The effect of confluence position on distance to a bridge and to land transport is reported as the first columns of the main table and its emergence over census years is plotted as a coefficient series, establishing when the asymmetry arose.

Pre-existing asymmetries are checked graphically by residualized nonparametric plots of historical outcomes around confluences, and ferry crossing locations proxied by place names are shown to be symmetric in an appendix figure.
The paper notes that the panel estimate is a variance-weighted average of heterogeneous effects and shows in an appendix figure which times and places receive the most implicit weight.

Tract-design robustness is a short titled subsection with paragraph headings (permutation tests, varying exclusion distance, state fixed effects and topography controls); each paragraph summarises the check in words and points to an appendix figure or table.
observations.locator: Section 4.3; Appendix Figures C17, C18; Appendix Table C3

observations.statement: Panel robustness paragraphs cover counties never building a bridge (spillover only), progressively more flexible regional time trends, first differences with linear trends, and alternative start and end dates; attenuation under richer trends is discussed rather than dismissed.
observations.locator: Section 5.3; Appendix Tables C8, C13, C14; Appendix Figure C26

observations.statement: To interpret attenuation when adding regional trends, the author computes the share of measurement error in the treatment implied by the attenuation under classical error assumptions, using auxiliary regressions described in a footnote and an appendix section.
observations.locator: Section 5.3 More flexible time trends; footnote 45; Appendix B; Appendix Table C13

observations.statement: Less conservative trend controls (county fixed effects only, or linear trends only) are shown to produce nonzero lead coefficients, used as an argument for the quadratic trend baseline.

Heterogeneity is reported by river segment and river bank, by rail versus road bridges, by halves of the study period, and by initial distance to a bridge, all in appendix tables and figures and motivated by where bridge access should matter most.
observations.locator: Section 4.2; Section 5.2; Appendix Tables C3, C10 to C12; Appendix Figure C23

observations.statement: A dedicated section extends both designs to secondary outcomes (urbanization, industry composition, housing, commuting, education, demographics) grouped under narrative headings; results are summarised verbally in the text and detailed only in appendix tables and figures.
observations.locator: Section 6; Appendix Figures C27 to C38; Appendix Tables C15 to C23

observations.statement: Agglomeration feedback is distinguished from direct infrastructure effects by re-estimating in first differences with lagged population density as a control, following an earlier literature approach.

Log-point coefficients are converted to percentage differences in the text, effects on income are scaled by effects on distance to obtain an implied elasticity and compared with the raw descriptive elasticity, and panel elasticities are translated into the effect of halving distance.
Effects on total activity are decomposed into population and per capita components by comparing land value and population responses, with a derived per capita proxy estimated in the appendix.
observations.locator: Section 5.2; footnote 44; Appendix Figure C22, Table C7

observations.statement: Three reasons the land value proxy likely understates effects are enumerated (measurement error, urban land undervaluation, absorption by fitted trends), and the direction of bias from ferry replacement is argued.

The author states that only the first few lag coefficients are identified because trends absorb persistent effects and the assumption is plausible only within a window of decades; tract-level historical data are unavailable, so placebo tests rely on county data.
The conclusion cautions that relative effects cannot reveal aggregate effects when relocation matters, that a structural model would be needed, and lists mechanisms the paper cannot distinguish.

The conclusion discusses that urban poverty and suburban wealth may be specifically American and sketches how patterns might differ in developing countries; the design's applicability elsewhere is suggested via satellite examples in the appendix.

The main graphical evidence is a multi-panel figure of residualized outcomes against signed river position with local linear fits, bootstrap bands and binned markers; figure notes state bandwidth, kernel, clustering, replications and sample.

Presentation combines maps of rivers, bridges and counties, an event-style coefficient plot with reversed axis explained in the text, a three-panel summary statistics table covering both samples, and significance stars at three conventional levels defined in table notes.
Appendix material is lettered (Appendix A data details, Appendix B measurement error derivation, Appendix C figures and tables numbered C1 onwards) and referenced parenthetically throughout the text.

The introduction previews results from both designs with magnitudes, discusses identification threats for each, then gives three numbered contributions, related literature with footnoted taxonomy of existing strategies, and a roadmap paragraph.

A descriptive correlations section motivates the problem, a history and data section precedes the designs, each design has its own strategy, results and robustness subsections, mechanisms follow both, and the extensive appendix carries most secondary results.

A data availability statement points to a Zenodo replication package with a DOI cited in the references, explains that ICPSR files cannot be redistributed but are free to member institutions, and that IPUMS full-count microdata are replaced by included county aggregates with recreation instructions.

Data are public-use administrative and census sources, hand-verified bridge records with satellite imagery, third-party replication data for market access and pollution, and place-name gazetteer records used as a proxy for ferry sites.
No statistical software is named; only the source of adapted spatial standard error code is credited.

A simulation appendix figure is used to show how a discontinuous bridge-building probability yields a continuous but asymmetric distance pattern that appears discontinuous once aggregated, explaining why the unit of observation matters.

concordance.paper_says: Reduced-form OLS of 2010 tract outcomes on downstream indicator with nearest-tributary fixed effects and river-distance controls interacted with downstream (equation 4.1).
concordance.card_shows: s1: reg outcome c.tribdist_signed##i.downstream with absorb(tempid2), est=ols.

concordance.paper_says: Nearest-tributary fixed effects absorb broad spatial trends.
concordance.note: tempid2 read as the nearest-tributary identifier.

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors cluster-bootstrapped by nearest tributary confluence with 1,000 replications.
concordance.card_shows: s1 records cluster(tempid2) analytic clustering; no bootstrap wrapper recorded in the traced line.
concordance.note: Cluster level agrees; SE type differs (bootstrap vs analytic cluster) as far as the card records. The bootstrap may be implemented around this call in code not captured by the card.

concordance.paper_says: Observations weighted by a triangular kernel in river-distance to nearest confluence.
concordance.note: Card does not record how weight is constructed.

concordance.paper_says: Exclusion threshold of 31.4 km chosen as the minimum of rdbwselect optimal bandwidths across three outcomes; robustness to varying it in Appendix Figure C18.
concordance.card_shows: x1 bandwidth_selection call present (rdbwselect, IK and CCD); sample condition tribdist < ${ex_dist}.

concordance.paper_says: Tracts within 10 km of the rivers, centroid within threshold of a confluence, confluences with at least two tracts; Ohio truncation and Mississippi upper limit stated.
A McCrary density test would fail by construction and is not reported (footnote 23).
County panel distributed lag model with year FE, county FE and county-specific quadratic trends, leads added in diagnostic columns (equation 5.1).
concordance.card_shows: s2: ols_spatial_cluster of outcome on lnbdist_diff leads 3..1, contemporaneous, lags 1..3, year dummies, county dummies, county x t and county x t2.

concordance.paper_says: Clustered by county and robust to spatial correlation within 200 km using Conley SEs adapted from Hsiang (2010).
concordance.card_shows: ols_spatial_cluster with distcutoff(200000), panelvar(icpsrfip), timevar(year); card se fields null.

NBI bridge records, NHGIS, ICPSR county files, IPUMS full count, USGS NHD and DEM, ESRI rivers.

gaps: No statistical software named in the text (Stata and MATLAB appear only in the replication package).
No R-squared or dependent variable mean reported in regression tables.
No balance table in the conventional tabular form; balance is graphical and via placebo outcomes.
No multiple testing adjustment mentioned despite many secondary outcomes in Section 6.
No preregistration or ethics statement (not applicable to archival data).
Online appendix (Appendices A, B, C) not included in the text file; appendix content known only through in-text references.

reading.note: All 33 pages of the published article read, including footnotes, table and figure notes, data availability statement and references. Appendices A to C are in the separate online supplement and were not available in the text file; their contents are recorded only as cited in the main text.
